The interim payment that I spoke of a moment ago will be quite a help to those farmers who were able to thresh and to deliver some of their grain. But for those who have not been able to thresh or combine grain and deliver it, there is little comfort in that payment. It leaves those people who did not have any grain threshed badly in need of the final payment on the five-year pool, 1945 to 1949, both years inclusive.
Many people still seem at a loss to understand why the farmers claim some compensation under that agreement. It must be readily understood that out of the 1946 crop, according to an agreement made between the Canadian government and the British government, Canada was to supply to Britain 160 million bushels of wheat at a price of $1.55. During that crop year the wheat board-for which I have the highest regard and which I shall support as long as I am here, knowing the difficulties and the losses that the grain exchange got us into in the past-was able to sell grain to countries other than Britain, for which they received $2.43 per bushel, which made a net loss of 88 cents a bushel on wheat that was sent to Britain. That means that any farmer who delivered 1,000 bushels for delivery to Britain had an immediate loss of $880. If he delivered 2,000 bushels, his loss directly on account of the agreement was $1,760. If he delivered 3,000 bushels, as many farmers did, he accepted a loss of $2,640.
In the next year we were again expected to deliver and did deliver 160 million bushels at $1.55 a bushel, according to the agreement. That year the wheat board sold class II wheat again to countries other than Britain, at an average price of $2.88 per bushel; so that the farmers again had to suffer a loss of $1.33 per bushel. To bring this situation nearer home, it means that the farmer who delivered 1,000 bushels for delivery to Britain suffered a loss of $1,330 right off the bat. If he delivered 2,000 bushels, his loss was $2,660; and if he delivered 3,000 bushels -and many of them delivered far more than that-his loss was $3,990. Yet many people ask us why the farmers are coming to the government begging for some more money. Mr. Speaker, I do not want anyone in this house or in Canada to feel that the farmers have ever begged the government for anything. But if by various methods they had not been robbed-and I use the word "robbed" advisedly-of the things they produced in this country, they would not be in the financial position in which they find themselves today in many parts of the country.
The Address-Mr. Fair
In 1948 we had agreed to deliver 140 million bushels, and the same in 1949, at a price of $2 per bushel. In 1948 the price for class II wheat was $2.23 a bushel. I am not able to give any figures in connection with the 1949 crop because those figures were not available the last time I asked for them, but I hope to get them in the near future. In addition to that, while by government contract we subsidized the people of Britain, we also subsidized the people of Canada in order that they could eat cheap bread for several years past. The loss sustained on that account and the loss sustained under the British wheat agreement in my opinion runs up fairly close to $600 million.
In speaking to the Saskatchewan wheat pool delegates in Regina a couple of months ago, the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that it would cost $14 million to pay one cent a bushel on the wheat during the five-year period. That is quite a good deal of money. But he did not say that payment of that amount would be borne by all of the people of Canada. He also neglected to point out the loss that the few thousand wheat growers in the prairie provinces will have to suffer as the result of that subsidizing of the British people and of the Canadian people.
Apparently the government is still negotiating with Britain. Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) mentioned questions that I had asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce, questions that the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) had asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce and questions that he himself had asked the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent); but with respect to which we were unable to get any particular information. In my opinion we should not, under the terms of the agreement, have asked Britain to pay a great deal. As for myself and those with whom I am associated here in the house, we believe that the job of making up those losses belongs to the people of Canada. At the time the Minister of Trade and Commerce was speaking to the Saskatchewan wheat pool delegates, or during that week anyway, a Liberal convention was held in Saskatoon, another city in Saskatchewan. At that time the leader of the Liberal party in that province, Mr. Walter Tucker, who was at one time the member for Rosthern, suggested to the convention that negotiations be reopened with Britain with respect to the "have regard" clause; and later in the convention a resolution was passed demanding that, and saying that if Britain did not make good, then the responsibility fell upon the Canadian government. Therefore I feel that we are in the company
128	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Fair of at least the Saskatchewan Liberals in demanding the repayment of the losses that we are pleading for here today.
At our convention held in Regina on October 18, 19 and 20-the convention of the Social Credit Association of Canada-a resolution was passed demanding that every dollar of this loss be made good out of the Canadian consolidated revenue fund.
I have read in the papers about the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), either or both of them, addressing delegates to the Alberta wheat pool convention in Calgary, the farmers' union of Alberta in Calgary, and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture also in Calgary; but in every instance not. much information was given. Before I leave this perhaps I had better state that I believe our farm leaders-I do not like to use this language-were just a little bit easy in dealing with this whole question of making up the losses. This is a business proposition, and the welfare, in fact the security, of a lot of the farmers in the prairie provinces is dependent upon the payments that will be made in this instance.
Facts that are not frankly faced have a habit of stabbing us in the back. That may possibly be worth thinking over. Conditions at the present time would indicate that in the very near future farmers may again be called upon to supply sons to fight Canada's battles on the battlefields of the world. They may also be called upon to supply sons and daughters to work in our munitions factories; they may be called upon to supply daughters to enlist in the three services, as was done in the last war. We may be asked to produce more and more food for ourselves and for our allies overseas. The conditions that have existed in agriculture up to the present time have been responsible for driving, and otherwise getting, 84,000 of our farm workers into the industrial centres during the past year. Perhaps this is worth thinking over also, because we should not have such a condition as that in agriculture in this country at the present time.
In connection with this final settlement on wheat in the 1945-49 wheat board pool, unless the farmers are treated properly they will not be so ready to respond to the government's request as they did in the last war. I am not suggesting that the farmers are going to do that, but do not forget that the farmers have a conscience. They demand a proper share of the production for which they are responsible in this country. Only during the years from 1915 to 1919 have the farmers ever received a proper share of the national income.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that in entering this debate there are certain aspects of our defence situation which possibly have not been touched upon previously and that at the present time are not thoroughly understood by the Canadian people from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
For a long time during the second world war different Canadians had occasion to say: "Well, it can't happen here." Consequently when today they are pondering in their minds the rather staggering figures that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) presented to this house in such an able manner last evening, they may be wondering just why this great expenditure of the taxpayers' money.
As I rise to take part in this debate I have two ideas in mind, one dealing with the question:	"It can't happen here," and the
other with the economics of our defencespending program. It is quite easy for a great number of people to understand what happens to their pocketbooks when taxation becomes heavy. That is a more understandable proposition with the great mass of Canadians than to say that our expenditure for, say, the construction of a certain type of aeroplane is $400,000; because to many of those within the range of my voice that is an astronomical figure.
Before I go further with the points that I have outlined I should like to say how pleased I was that the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) was batting substantially on our side yesterday.
I should also like to pay my respects to the remarks made by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) who, as hon. members know, has a most distinguished war record. He was a colonel when I was a rear rank buck private in the first world war. At that time my highest ambition would have been reached if I could have attained half the number of medals that General Pearkes had. If I could have obtained them I would have been satisfied, but I never obtained any of them. I trust I may be excused, sir, if I refer specifically to his remarks about the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry. I might also be pardoned if I make this statement:	I was one of five brothers who
served all during the first world war. One of them was more or less a poet. He was then living in the United States of America, which at that time had not entered the war. He composed a little poem, of which I shall quote only one verse. I do so, sir, not only in honour of the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, but in honour of all our armed services who were serving and have served in all parts of the world.

That little verse went something like this:
Tell me, Canucks, who are these Pats?
Who are these boys In the broad-brimmed hats?
Who are these soldier lads off to the front Eager to bear and share in the brunt?
Quick to respond to Canada's call Smarting to fight and ready to fall?
Why, those are the boys of the regiment that Is Canada's glory-the Princess Pats.
My reference a few minutes ago to the statement, "It can't happen here" was prompted by a document I have before me which, with the permission of the house, I should like to place on record. It is an exact copy of the Hitlerian edict that eliminated the independent non-state church in Germany in 1933.
Dictators, whether of today, fifty years ago or a thousand years ago, are ostensibly one and the same thing. A definition, the author of which I cannot name, states that a dictator is any man who claims to have power over the conscience of man and, having that power, if he could, would usurp the kingdom of God. We have today in the world the type of individual we had in the years immediately preceding and subsequent to the termination of the second world war.
It is because of this fact that I wish to place this document on record, so that it may give an insight, in the minds of those who hear and read, to the fact that what happened in 1933 with respect to Christian tenets of faith in Germany can happen here, provided we are not prepared to spend our dollars in defence of our freedom and our belief in the Christian faith.
This document is in these words:
The Program' of the National Church (Reichskirche) of Germany
1.	The national church (Reichskirche) of Germany claims with all clearness the exclusive right and the exclusive power on all churches within the boundaries of the German empire. These churches will be nominated "national churches of the German Reich."
2.	The German people is not supposed to serve the national church of the German Reich, the national church of the German Reich has to serve exclusively and solely to one doctrine "people and race."
3.	The territory for working and activity of the national church of the German Reich will be marked' by the territorial empire and colonial frontiers of Germany.
4.	The national church of the German Reich will not force any German individual, to join, she is, however, willing to do everything within her might, to get hold even of the last German soul. Other churches or similar institutions and associations may and will not be tolerated in Germany, especially if they are internationally bound or directed.
5.	The national church of the German Reich has decided to eradicate unalterably and with all necessary means the Christian faith, which was imported in the disastrous year 800 into Germany, which was
The Address-Mr. MacDougall pressed on the German people, although it was against its nature and not identical to its character.
6.	There will be not allowed any fundamental changement in the construction of the existing church buildings because they represent German national property, German culture and a part of the historical growing of our German people. They will not only have the value of the German national property, but they also must be preserved.
7.	In the national church of the German Reich there will be no scribers, ministers, chaplains and clergymen, but only public speakers of the national church of the German Reich.
8.	The celebrations of the national church of the German Reich will take place at night and not in the morning, that is to say on Saturdays, at splendid illumination.
9.	In the national church of the German Reich men and women, boys and girls will acknowledge unanimous God and His immortal works.
10.	The national church of the German Reich insists firmly upon her unfailing fusion with the state. She has to subordinate herself to the state as a serving member.
11.	On the strength of this fusion she demands an immediate delivery of all territorial property of all churches and confessions to the state. She interdicts, also, that in future the churches will not be allowed to own the smallest part of the earth, or that such a part will be given to them, for the churches do not conquer, defend and build the German estate and soil, but only the German people: "The State".
12.	The national church speakers will never be chosen among those who constantly talk today with malice 3Ud tricks in words and writing about the absolute necessity and maintenance of the Christian doctrine in Germany, for they not only deceive themselves but also the German people and only on account of their position and their "sugar bread".
13.	The national church speakers will officiate as German state officials after the law and state-officials.
14.	The national church of the German Reich demands the immediate stoppage of the printing and publishing of the bible within the boundary of Germany as well as some more publishing of Sunday papers, writing, readings of church-similar character.
15.	The national church of the German Reich has to superintend with all severity at that, and she has to take strictest measures that the holy bible and other Christian religious scriptures cannot be imported to Germany.
I believe it is well that the people of Canada should have this authentic record of what dictatorship has done in one of the former great states of the world. That should be some indication to the people of Canada, whether within or without the halls of parliament, that what has happened in Germany can, save by the grace of God, happen to the people of Canada. I am sure, sir, none of us wishes to see that occur in this beautiful land. It has been our good fortune that the Almighty has placed us geographically whereby, in two world holocausts, we have avoided the actual bombings and carnage of war, and have suffered only the loss of our dear ones on the fields of battle.
I believe it was Sir Wilfrid Laurier who, many years ago, in describing the geographical boundaries of Canada, said: "It is
130	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. MacDougall bounded on the north by gold; on the west by the east; on the south by friends and on the east by history." Certainly that describes our geographical position. How fortunate we are. Right here I should like to say that I believe earnestly the countenances of our Canadian people should be a great deal more smiling than they are today. So many people that we meet seem to think that we are being hard done by. Our cup is running over and yet we are not satisfied. In this time of world chaotic conditions it would seem to me that we individually and collectively would profit ourselves by the recognition of the fact that we have been favoured under Providence and that a smile on our lips would be a great national emblem for us to bear no matter where we may be, whether at home or abroad. Certainly sugar draws more flies than vinegar. I think we should all practise for ourselves and preach among our neighbours that the happy heart is a treasure to possess and also a treasure with which to associate.
Coming now to the scope of our national program and its economic problems I should like to quote, something which I do not like to do but which I have done quite consistently today, an editorial that appeared in a small British Columbia publication known as the B.C. Financial Times. I do not suppose that many easterners have heard of that publication. In its issue of January it had what to me was a very sound and sensible article with respect to our national defence spending. I should like to quote this as it will take only a matter of five or six minutes. It reads:
The essence of the economic problem is the release of heavy and sustained government expenditure of an unproductive character on a situation where factors of inflation are already active. This has to be recognized as a continuing state of affairs, though quite unlike the intensive effort of 1940-45 when every normal activity was subordinated to winning the war. Open war may come; but if it can be avoided, these conditions will probably go on for years and we have to decide how we can live with them and survive them most advantageously. It has been well said that one of democracy's difficulties is that the future has no vote, so that the national interest is too easily identified with what the majority of people want here and now. Our problem is that most people are going to want things that cannot be provided in these circumstances.
Objectives of Policy
The policy required to meet this situation must embrace two objectives: (1) increased production; and (2) economic stability.
I am happy to say that the government has recognized that fundamental fact.
These are inseparable. Stability means an underlying balance between spending and supply. Defence supply will certainly get priority. Consequently, civilian supply may or may not be reduced


long-term, but civilian demand will be much augmented by transfusion of government expenditure and this will happen at once. Two lines of approach are therefore necessary.
The government is also cognizant of this.
The first is to continue to increase the production of civilian goods. The second is to channel excess purchasing power out of the market by taxation and saving.
Inflation is our opponent's secret weapon. It was Lenin who invented the slogan, "Debauch the currency first." Our defence therefore has two fronts. If we ignore the internal front of production and stability, the external front will prove to be another Maginot line.
At first sight there may seem to be a choice of two methods. One is to impose direct controls over prices and wages, and to allocate resources by government direction. The other is to encourage the vitality of an open economy, relying on its productive power and allowing the price system to do its work properly, protecting it from inflation and distortion by means of the indirect method! of fiscal and monetary control.
There is really no choice. Comprehensive direct controls would defeat the purpose in the following ways:	They would drive the economy into a
regime of black markets and administrative paralysis; would destroy public morale and the incentive to produce, and would conceal inflation without preventing it. They would in any event require crushing taxation to be practical at all.
The method of control, is, of course, necessary in order to allocate scarce materials to direct defence production. Its use in Canada will depend largely on what is done in the United States, in view of our joint supply arrangements with them. But there may be little need of formal apparatus in this country, provided that we succeed in the main object of controlling inflation at the source and can impress the American authorities with the vigour of our determination.
The second course indicated above spells control in an entirely different sense. It means that we can have a free economy so long as it does not run out of control. More particularly, it means that the government must conduct its budgetary operations in such a way that they add the least amount of fuel to the inflation process and exert a stabilizing influence upon it as far as possible. The indirect method of fiscal and monetary policy is therefore not only the right prescription, but it also offers the only assurance that the alternative of full "controls" can be avoided.
I should like in a word or two to express my opinion of the soundness of that editorial. If I may, I should also like to add my commendation of the government for the sane practical manner in which they have dealt with the present crisis while in some other countries hysteria has run rampant. We have heard a considerable amount of criticism of our reserve forces. I do not think that even the minister would say that he was entirely satisfied with the situation with respect to the reserve forces. We can and must continue to attract a greater number of our men and women throughout the country to the ranks of the reserve army.
There is something more I might add with respect to this matter. No one in this house, no one on the North American continent or in any of the other free countries of the

world knows when Uncle Joe may pull the trigger. The best that can be said for all our planning is that we may, by good fortune, be ready with our maximum endeavour at the time that is most emergent. I do not know whether he might pull the trigger in 1952, 1954 or 1956. That is in the lap of the gods. But I do know that, if this twilight cool war should not break into a flaming, open, shooting war, in all probability some time will elapse before the emergency becomes completely and utterly emergent in its fullest sense. Therefore if a period of years should be given to us to strengthen ourselves so that the potential aggressor will be rather shy of putting out his jaw for a haymaker it would seem to me that we could utilize most advantageously Canada's three services, the army, navy and air force, and additional endeavours could be made with respect to the recruitment of cadets in these various services.
As in the first world war, modern war is a young man's game. That is an accepted fact in practically all the countries of the world. When that is realized I think it is correct to assume that any additional enticement that we and the government of Canada may be able to offer for increased enlistment in cadet training will eventually pay off most handsomely for all the people of this country in a dire emergency.
Many of you within the range of my voice knew and loved as I did the old padre of the first world war, Canon Scott. The third time that I was wounded, I remember, Canon Scott came to my bedside on his horse over shell holes for a distance of twelve miles, not particularly to see me but to see three of us who were lying in a dressing station. One was a Protestant, one was a Roman Catholic, and one was a Jew. They were members of my battalion which we jokingly referred to at reunions as the fighting 46th that never took a trench and never lost one.
Since those days Canon Scott has passed to his last reward. I thought I should like to pay my tribute to that great Christian gentleman in ending my dissertation by utilizing a little verse that he wrote. In it he used the word "rest" but I am going to substitute the word "peace". I think this verse is a fine motto for us in these troublesome times and that we should think of the things that are beyond dollars and cents. On that note I wish to conclude by quoting Canon Scott's verse, which is as follows:
To labour not for place or power,
Nor wealth which lasts a paltry hour,
But only that when peace is won,
A kindly God may say "Well done."
The Address-Mr. Poulin (Translation):

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make my humble contribution to the debate on the address in reply. I should indeed be remiss in my duty if I failed to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address for their excellent speeches, as did others who spoke before me. I am sure their constituents will be proud of their new representatives.
The top question in the speech from the throne is, of course, that of international relations and the position of the various delegates at the United Nations.
The American representatives at the UNO, amongst others, have shown a feverish eagerness. One would think that they have hastened to create conditions which are apt to bring about a general war.
What is their purpose? Did they ever state it clearly? Obviously, like everybody else, they are anxious to fight communism. Why then did they ostracize General Franco for so long?
Why did we not help nationalist China to the end? Why did we, only recently, side with Tito of Yugoslavia, a communist as dangerous as Stalin, to whom we shall have, sooner or later, to make compromising concessions, similar to those from which Stalin benefited at the end of the last war?
The American government undoubtedly wishes to maintain peace and order in the world under the aegis of the United Nations. At the time of the Korean incident, on June 27, 1950, why did the leaders of that country adopt a definite policy, even before the security council had taken a decision, and why did the latter, faced with a fait accompli, simply give its approval and blessing?
Yet in the case of Formosa, for example, the American government does not seem to mind risking widespread warfare, through its uncompromising attitude. In fact, we all know that Washington's assistant delegate to Lake Success asserted, on January 20 last, that the attitude of the United States would be dictated by the needs of their national security.
What explains the stubborn hurry with which American diplomats replied to China's counter-proposals during the past few weeks when the special committee of three, of which our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) was a member, very

The Address-Mr. Poulin commendably tried to temporize and to continue discussions in an attempt to find grounds for agreement.
I also believe it my duty to congratulate Canada's representative to the United Nations on the most acceptable and commendable stand he took on that occasion. It would be unfair not to offer the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the tribute of my personal approval of his attitude in inviting India's president to intervene and ask China to clarify her reply.
I have no illusions, knowing full well that by praising or censuring these hon. gentlemen I neither add to nor take away from their personal merit nor from the prestige they enjoy in the world. As an independent member of the house, I am duty-bound to adopt such an attitude.
For the moment, it would seem that the intervention of our representatives was not effective, but no one is willing to believe that their devotion and their efforts, especially those of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, will remain fruitless. Even if the effect of his plans is not yet generally felt, sooner or later we will realize that our Secretary of State for External Affairs meant well when, particularly the last few months, he sought peaceful settlement of this burning question. However, I am sorry that, by his vote on the American proposal to brand China an aggressor, our representative went back on the splendid work he had done for some months past. I also express the hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will agree to be a member of the new committee now being planned to discuss the situation with the Peking government.
Why then should the United States representatives be so anxious to have China called an aggressor, knowing that this will, in effect, make further negotiation impossible, whatever may be said and whatever the house may think to the contrary, as has been proven in the past few days?
And now, to be logical, our behaviour towards China, an aggressive power, should be the same as our behaviour towards North Korea, also an aggressive power. Otherwise it will be thought that the United Nations' attitude towards smaller countries is not the same as towards great powers. It is easy to see the impossible situation

into which we have been thrust by the warlike ardour of our neighbours. Their intentions may be pure, but they want to drag us along with them, in good fortune or ill.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while she plays an important part in world affairs England is not prepared to rush matters. She evidently wants to protect her interests, her assets and her crown colonies in Asia.
Indeed her history shows that England has no friends; she has only interests. She knows, however, that she must look after them herself and trust to no one to do it for her. Be that as it may, what has been the result of this policy? England continues to avoid war and, to that end, strives to prevent interventions in Asia.
Besides, except for the great influence exerted by Washington on the decisions taken at the United Nations, it must necessarily be admitted that the large majority of countries want no part in an adventure that may lead to a general war.
Forces were sent to save Korea, and now we know how many unforgiveable blunders were made in this adventure on behalf of free nations. Shall we conitnue risking a war with China, a country that the United States will never be able to conquer or subdue? What Japan could not do within range of its cannons, western nations cannot do from thousands of miles away.
Moreover it must not be forgotten that under the present circumstances communism in China is perhaps but the manifestation of her nationalism, and that in order to get that country out of Moscow's orbit, shelling with butter would be much more effective than with guns.
China is now a communist country, not on principle or from conviction, but rather on grounds of expediency, out of necessity, because she cannot live otherwise. Let us give her a chance to recover, to rehabilitate herself, to find her lost freedom. Let us grant her a seat at the United Nations and we may have the great satisfaction of witnessing a change of attitude on her part. She will not become an ally of the western nations. On the contrary, she will no longer be the unwilling ally of Russian imperialism. She will be once again a nationalist and

traditionalist country. What could be better for peace in Asia and in the world than the materializing of such a possibility?
The policy followed by the United Nations, and especially Washington, is leading to a world war by the reaction it draws from the Russians who, obviously, in their own interest, help communist China. One would even think that war is being prepared.
The monstrous war budget of $87 billion introduced by the American government and Canada's defence plan calling for an expenditure of $5 billion lead us strongly to believe that a general war is in the offing. These fabulous expenditures, I will be told, are designed to prevent war. As was done last September, the old saying si vis Tpacem, para helium, if you want peace, prepare for war, will be invoked. But history proves this saying to be false; conquerors have always used it as a sham to hide their infamous designs for conquest. History is repeating itself once more. Besides, we all know that this saying was coined by these same people, these same imperialists who preached a preventive war of conquest with these words: delenda est Carthago, Carthage must be destroyed.
The Roman empire then wanted, in the name of peace, to cross the Mediterranean and destroy the very foundations of the African empire. Today the American empire is picking up the torch from the failing hands of the British empire and wants to cross not only the Mediterranean but the seven seas and use guns, tanks and flame throwers to make the Asiatic people benefit from the blessings of peace. And they want to drag Canada into the venture: we are already taking part in the undertaking as members of the Atlantic pact organization that has been set up.
We are asked to defend Europe or to defend ourselves in Europe. The speech from the throne suggests-and this was confirmed Monday by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Clax.ton)-that the house will be called upon to vote billions of dollars for war or defence preparations.
In addition, Canada is being asked to send troops to the eventual battlefield of Europe. What shall we do in Canada? How shall we defend ourselves? Who will defend us and with what weapons?
We are told that the European continent is, at present, hard to defend against a mass Russian attack. In the event of such an
The Address-Mr. Poulin attack and of the possible fall of Europe, the American continent would become vulnerable. That, in my humble opinion, means that we should get ready to defend our own country. We should keep in Canada all the men available.	We should also use
the millions and the billions of dollars that will be voted by this house to organize our own protection.
I am neither a military man nor a tactician; when the first world war was declared, I was too young to take part in it and when the last one ended, I was no longer young enough to serve. I shall however be allowed to form a personal opinion, especially since I compel no one to concur in it. I do not share the view of those who claim we can defend Europe any more than I agree with those who would have us believe Canada can eventually be invaded, even if I admit that she can be attacked.
However, to save our country from such a disaster we must keep in this country the forces at our disposal and which we would need in case of attack, instead of sending them to Europe, where they probably would be destroyed without any tangible result. For, in the final analysis, results are what count.
In 1939, we fought a war to save Poland and thus keep a promise made to one of our allies. What were the results of our intervention? We have won the war, yet Poland is now subject to the worst kind of slavery she has ever known throughout the whole of her extremely tragic history.
We know now what our intervention in foreign wars can lead to. Already, from various districts across Canada come suggestions, urgent appeals for the conscription of our manpower for compulsory military service. This concerted pressure will go on increasing and well do we know what happened in the past under similar conditions: the government, whether Conservative or Liberal, finally yielded.
We will send to Europe or to Asia as many men as we will be able to recruit. When at last our country finds itself face to face with imminent danger-which heaven forbid-we will be told that conscription is necessary since we lack soldiers for our own defence.
Let us keep the soldiers at home that we can raise through voluntary enlistment. Let us not send them abroad to die probably in vain. And, after that, if the danger should grow greater and more pressing, so that we would need more men for our own defence,

The Address-Mr. Poulin there is not a single man worthy of the name-and that would include the humble representative from the constituency of Beauce-who would refuse to serve or to lay down his life in defence of his country!
The speech from the throne announces our continued participation in the Colombo plan for aid to underdeveloped countries. That is a very laudable plan which should not provoke too much discussion, as far as the principle is concerned, at any rate. For my part, I am entirely in favour of it.
If we are to fight communism, and I think we must fight it, I know of no better way of doing it successfully. Let us raise the standards of living in underdeveloped countries and their citizens will be much more inclined to shun communistic theories than if we resorted to bombing.
However, it should be borne in mind that, according to the gospel, "Man shall not live by bread alone." We should do our best to develop learning, education and religion among those peoples, all of them being free to improve their standards according to and along the lines of their national aspirations. Let us not try to change them into occidentals, because it would be useless; besides we would thus encourage their present tendency to turn towards Russia, which could be easily understood as a natural move of caution on their part. And above all, let us not make the colossal blunder of providing these populations with arms and munitions that they might very well turn against us.
Besides, those nations should be deeply impressed with the fact that western civilization is based more on fundamental principles and truths to liberate the mind than on weapons to enslave the body. Briefly, let us strive to make them love constructive peace rather than destructive war.
For some weeks past, I have endeavoured to poll the opinion of the constituents of Beauce with respect to the Canadian military budget.
I am convinced that the great majority of them have been startled by the announcement of a $5 billion budget.
I trust that in the future the supporters of an all-out effort will be satisfied and that a certain Montreal newspaper will stop showing the Minister of National Defence with a wooden sword and a straw cap.

On February 1, the leader of the official opposition moved an amendment to the speech from the throne. I cannot accept paragraphs 1 and 2 because, in my humble opinion, they are couched in terms too vague. Had it not been for the last paragraph, I would certainly have voted against the amendment. However, that last paragraph warrants my full and spontaneous support. It reads as follows:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to take effective measures to combat inflation and the rapidly rising cost of living.
Mr. Speaker, when one thinks of the high cost of living, when one notices that the rise in the cost of living is proportionately much higher for the poor man than for the rich, because of the very fact that it affects consumer goods that the poor cannot do without, such as food and clothing, let us also stop and think that the government may be planning to bring in controls that would freeze prices at their present level while salaries, which have not increased at the same rate, will also be frozen at a relatively low level. In view of all these considerations, I cannot help supporting and voting for the amendment even though the first two paragraphs do not suit me.
The subamendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) recognizes that the government has followed a constructive course in relation to the Korean dispute. I do not share this view and I said so emphatically in the house on September 2 last. With this qualification, however, I shall vote for this subamendment because it censures the government, and with good reason I believe, for having supported a course which is premature and unwise in relation to the resolution branding China as an aggressor.
Before concluding my remarks I wish to add a word about the national flag which Canada, like all self-respecting countries, should have.
On November 17 and 18 last I attended two beautiful ceremonies at St. George and St. Joseph de Beauce in commemoration of the Canadians who gave their lives in the two world wars, among whom were many men from the county of Beauce. At both places the ceremonies were moving and well carried out and I wish to congratulate the organizers.
At one of those places a scene was enacted in which some distinguished veterans of Beauce county mounted guard around the body of a Canadian soldier who had fallen on the field of honour. This Canadian soldier who had died for his country and who was

surrounded by some of his compatriots who had generously offered their lives was wrapped up in a shroud which seemed to me like a flag but on which I looked in vain for something recalling the country for which this Canadian had given up his life. For once in my life I admit I was ashamed of my country, for having failed so far to give those who die for their fatherland a shroud which would not be an insult to the greatness of their sacrifice. And all those who were there took advantage of that occasion to request the government of Canada to give its citizens at last a national flag.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (St. John's West):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my congratulations to the mover of the address to be presented to His Excellency for the speech with which this session was opened. May I thank the hon. member, first, for the reference he made to the Labrador iron ore mines. Like him, I hope that it may not be long before we shall see, as one speaker said last year, "the giant iron ore carriers moving up the St. Lawrence loaded with iron ore from the Labrador ore fields."
Tonight I do not think I should make any apology for drawing the discussion away from the subject that has been followed generally thus far by speakers in the debate. For a few minutes I shall deal with conditions in Newfoundland. So many people have asked me what things are like in Newfoundland that I think I should make some remarks in this connection.
A few days ago we had the pleasure of learning that the board of transport commissioners had given a decision in favour of Newfoundland's case, stating that the freight rates that had been charged since April 1, 1949, had been excessive, and that they had been contrary to the terms of union between the two countries. This decision however was not made retroactive. The effect of it was to make Newfoundlanders think that during almost two years excessive rates had been charged, and that moneys at the rate of $4 million a year had been collected by the Canadian National Railways in excess of what should have been collected. The excess amounted to almost $7 million.
I would suggest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) that justice requires retribution in such a case. A good opportunity is now open to the minister to make such retribution. I believe he has been in receipt of correspondence from the board of trade
The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne in St. John's, Newfoundland, requesting that, in the construction of the ferry now being planned to carry passengers, goods and motor vehicles across the Cabot strait from North Sydney to Port aux Basques, there should be provision for carrying goods by freight cars as was done in connection with the ferry from the mainland to Prince Edward Island.
At the present time I understand there is a wide-gauge track on Prince Edward Island. In Newfoundland we have a narrow-gauge track of three feet six inches, while the mainland gauge is over four feet six inches. In the early days of Prince Edward Island it was the custom to carry the freight cars across on the ferry, lay the freight car with the wide-gauge alongside the freight car with the narrow-gauge, and transfer the goods from one car to the other. Let us see what happens at the present time-and this is one place where the traffic is almost entirely in one direction, with Newfoundland purchasing $100 million worth of goods from the other nine provinces, and the other nine provinces purchasing not more than about $10 million worth from Newfoundland.
The freight goes down in the freight cars to North Sydney. It has to be taken ou of the freight cars and put into sheds. Then it has to be taken out of the sheds and put on steamers so that it can be brought to Port aux Basques. There it is taken out of steamers and put into sheds, following which it is taken out of sheds and put into the freight cars. Would it not be very much better, when the minister is arranging the design of the ferry boat, to have it so that freight cars can be placed on it, travelling across from North Sydney to Port aux Basques, so that when reaching Port aux Basques the goods could be placed directly from the freight cars with the wide gauge to the freight cars with the narrow gauge.
I understand from the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield), who has a great deal of interest in matters of transport, as the minister knows, that this is a practical proposition. I trust the minister may see his way clear to kill two birds with one stone so as to do justice to Newfoundland, following the excessive rates which have been taken from that province in the last twenty months. I believe justice could be done by providing us with a service which will be satisfactory for many years to come. If trade with the other provinces of Canada is to flourish and grow, as I hope it will, he will have to make such provision, or he will be left with a boat he will not know what to do with-because I do not think the trade would grow so fast that

The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne he could use two boats at the same time. He is going to invest a certain amount of money in this ferry boat. I believe there has been mention of the sum of $8 million. If that is so, then very careful consideration should be given to the question before a final decision is made.
What are the conditions in Newfoundland at the present time? Apart from our fishing industry we have a pulp and paper industry, with the largest pulp and paper mill in the world, located at Corner Brook. We have another large paper mill at Grand Falls. We have a composite ore mine at Buchan's owned, I believe, by the American Smelting and Mining Company. We have a great iron ore hematite mine at Bell island, in Conception bay. I am very glad to be able to say that, although unfortunately it is on account of war conditions, an extra order for a million tons of ore has been received by the Dominion Steel Company for the export of iron ore from Bell island, which will give much employment in the district represented by my hon. friend from St. John's East (Mr. Higgins). I am very glad that he has that prosperity in his district, and I am sure that my district, too, will benefit to some extent from it. The paper mills are working to capacity. In addition to that, orders have been received from the United Kingdom for the export of large quantities of pulpwood.
In addition to these industries we receive, due to confederation, the benefits of family allowances, old age pensions, and unemployment insurance, and we also have the benefits introduced by the provincial government in the form of mothers' allowances and dependents' allowances on a scale which we did not have before.
But, sir, making due allowance for all these sources of revenue, and for the prosperity that must ensue from the extension of the industries I have mentioned, there still remains the great fishing industry which, for centuries, has been the staple industry of my country. If the fisheries in Newfoundland prosper, then the whole of the country is prosperous. If the fisheries are not prosperous, then the province cannot be said to be prosperous, and people cannot be said to be happy. They become discontented, critical and discouraged.
What has been the experience in the last year? Perhaps hon. members would like tc know. Some may recall that it was necessary for the Canadian government to give a subsidy in respect of the fish left over and not sold from the 1949 catch. The industry started the year 1950 with that quantity of fish on hand, which the government bought. I do not think they bought much, because they did not take what was in the hands of


the merchants, and accepted only what was in the hands of the fishermen. I do not think the subsidy came to a great amount of money. But here is what the fisherman had to face after he had reluctantly decided to take part in the 1950 fishing season at the urging of the provincial premier.
In the first place the fisherman had to face a reduction of almost $3.50 per quintal of fish, or from $13.95 down to $10.50, with prices for the lower grades in proportion. That was a drop of over three cents per pound in the price of fish. These prices were paid in September in the early season, but as the season advanced the price began to drop lower, and dropped fast. Some of the merchants did not wish to buy Labrador fish. I do not know whether it was because of the representations made by the provincial government or because we have a Newfoundlander as a member of the government, but the federal government came forward and guaranteed a price of $7 per quintal for the Labrador catch. People were discouraged last year from going to Labrador. Others had sold their vessels, but the total catch was only about 150,000 quintals.
What about the shore fishery, which is the principal part of our fisheries? The catch there amounted to about 800,000 quintals. What was the attitude of the government in reference to that? The government did not give any guarantee but simply said they would keep the matter under review, would keep a close watch on it. But the government has done nothing about it. The fisherman of Newfoundland could not afford to wait for weeks or months until the government made up its mind and so perforce he had to sell his fish at depressed prices.
Not only was the normal price $3.50 a quintal lower, but the fish were culled in such a way by the merchants as to give much lower prices. If a merchant did not want to buy fish he would say it was poor quality and would put it in a lower grade. If a fisherman was sufficiently disgruntled or angry he might persuade the merchant to cull his fish a little higher. I was told by an outport planter that one fisherman had brought thirty quintals of fish to a merchant and these were first culled as being 25 quintals low-grade fish and five quintals of what we call madeira, for which the price was about $10.50 per quintal. He became angry and threatened to take the matter up with the inspectors in St. John's and the merchant changed his mind and made a second cull which turned out at 15 quintals of good quality fish and 15 quintals of lower quality. The fisherman still was not satisfied. He cursed and swore and said he was going to St. John's to get someone to come over

to see what was being done. His fish was culled the third time and this time the result was 25 quintals of good fish with only five quintals of lower quality.
This outport planter said to me that he had written to the fisheries board in St. John's, which is the representative of the Department of Fisheries, and asked what they were going to do. He wanted to know if there were three different ways of culling or grading fish. He has not yet received an answer. I fear there are more than three ways of culling fish. A lot depends upon the attitude taken by the merchant.
I have seen many receipts given by merchants for the 1949 and 1950 catches. I know that in 1949 almost all the fish was culled as being high grade and the top price paid was $13.95 per quintal. But in 1950 most of the fish was culled as being of an inferior grade. I have here copies of receipts that were passed over to me by fishermen. One fisherman said to me, "Why is the federal government guaranteeing the price of Labrador fish and not guaranteeing the price of shore fish? Don't you think that the people who fish from the shores of Newfoundland deserve as much consideration as those who fish in Labrador waters? What is the difference between the two?"
I have no complaint to make about the Labrador fishermen receiving a guaranteed price, but what about these shore fishermen? I do not suppose there are many hon. members outside of those who come from Newfoundland who understand the difference between the two types of fishing. Labrador fishing is normally carried on from a vessel and the fishermen are not able to dry the fish so well. It therefore contains more moisture. The shore fisherman is able to dry his fish more carefully and it has a higher value. Generally shore fish are worth from $3 to $5 more per quintal than the Labrador fish.
The guaranteed price for Labrador fish was $7 per quintal and you would therefore expect that the price received by the shore fisherman would be in the neighbourhood of $10 per quintal. What did he receive? As I said a moment ago the fishermen were asking why they did not have a guarantee for their fish. I sat down and wrote to the minister and the minister wrote back saying that he was informed that the price being received by the fishermen ranged between $9 and $10.50 per quintal. He was surprised to hear the figures \vhich I quoted. I have in my hand receipts of the same date that the minister wrote, November 21, and also some of the same date on which I received his letter, November 27. As I say, the minister 80709-10
The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne was quite surprised at the figures I had quoted in my letter, namely, $5.30 and $4 per quintal.
As I said a moment ago, the price which the minister thought was being paid was between $9 and $10.50 per quintal. He had received that information from the St John's fisheries board. I called up the fisheries board and found that that was also their impression. As a result I do not think very much of the fisheries board. I do not think they talk to the fishermen at all; I think they talk only to the merchants. They take what the merchants have set as the price for fish, not what is actually paid. Anyway, that was the information given to the minister by the fisheries board.
I have one receipt here averaging $8.10 which is the highest price paid. That was on September 9, at the beginning of the season. Here is one for September 19 averaging $6.50. Here is one for October 17 for $3.75. Here is one November 27, the date I received the letter from the minister, for $5.90. The average for all this man's fish is $6.20, which is over $3 below the lowest price the minister thought was being paid, and 80 cents below the guaranteed price for Labrador fish.
I have another lot of receipts, one for November 13 and one for November 17, the date on which I wrote to the minister. The receipt for November 13 shows a price of $4.90, and the one for November 17, $5.42. This is an average of $5.16 a quintal or $4 below the price the minister thought the fishermen were receiving. Here is another lot of receipts showing an average price of $5.50 per quintal; here is another lot showing an average price of $5.50. The gentleman who gave me these told me that the same fish would have fetched $13 per quintal in 1949. He said that 448 quintals had been sold by him at an approximate average of $5.50 per quintal. I took this matter very seriously because I wanted to bring the matter up in the house when I came here for it is a matter of the greatest consequence to the fishermen of Newfoundland. I got in touch with some fishermen on whose judgment and opinion I thought I could rely. I talked to several and asked them to give me their candid opinions, and one man in particular wrote. Here are the prices that he gives: $7 for the large madeira, which is the best quality that is being sold this year; $6 50 for the small; $5 for the large West India and $4.50 for the small West India. He said the fish was sold at an average of approximately $6 per quintal, which is $1 per quintal less than the price paid by the government for

The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne Labrador fish, and as much as $4.50 less than the price which the minister thought was being paid as the top price for shore fish.
The fishermen were very discouraged and disheartened this year, and they said to me that they were not going to fish next year. They were persuaded to do so this year against their better judgment because they felt if there was not a guarantee given them they would lose money on what they were doing. This one man said to me in his letter:
I might add this price is no good for fish and unless something is done for this year to guarantee at least $9 or $10 per quintal for dried shore fish X do not see that there will be many fishing. For my own part I operate cod traps and unless there is a price set X cannot see how I can go fishing, and this goes for a great many.
I do not want to read any more of the letter. That represents the general opinion. Several fishermen have told me that they have burned their flakes. We have heard the expression "burned their boats". These men have burned their flakes. It amounts to the same thing because it means they have no place where they can dry their fish. There is no industry in Newfoundland which is more important for the prosperity of the country than fishing. That is generally recognized because, while you may have one Bell island, one Buchan's, one Grand Falls and one Comer Brook, where thousands of men are employed, there are in Newfoundland another thousand settlements at least where men are fishing, and only a comparatively small proportion of them are engaged in fishing and selling their fish fresh. The majority of them are dependent on the sale of salt codfish.
You might be interested to know what happened to that fish; and every fisherman in my riding and in Newfoundland generally would like to know what happens to the fish after it has been sold to the merchant. One man came into my office and said he did not know what he was going to do with his fish. He had 80 quintals of fish. He sold it and it netted him $5.30. As we say, it was bought sight unseen. What was the average price of that fish when it was sent to the markets abroad? Our fish goes to Puerto Rico, Jamaica, the Barbados, Spain, Portugal and Italy. I was glad to see that the other day UNICEF, a United Nations organization, bought 500 tons of fish for Yugoslavia and Greece. I should like to know how much they paid for it.
Today I got in touch with the dominion bureau of statistics and found out the average price paid for all fish exported from Canada in October, November and December, and if the averages are fair and just in one particular, they ought to be fair and just in

the other. For October the average price was 14-6 cents per pound. For November the average price was 12-7 cents per pound, and for December 16 cents per pound. The best part of our fish goes to Puerto Rico, a larger proportion than to any other foreign market, and the average price in December for fish that went to that country was 15 cents per pound.
A great deal of that fish came from Newfoundland because Newfoundland is the greatest salt codfish exporting province in Canada. In contrast to the 14-6 cents received in October, 3J-7J cents was paid to the fishermen. In contrast with the 12-7 cents in November, less than 6 cents was paid to the fishermen, and in contrast to the 16 cents in December, on December 8 the average price paid to some fishermen was less than 5 cents a pound when the average export price going through customs, as recorded by the dominion bureau of statistics, was 16 cents a pound.
It needs no great imagination to see that between 5 or 6 or 7 cents a pound and 16 cents a pound there is a great gap. I am sorry the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) is not present. I know he would like to hear what I am saying, and I hope he will find time to read it in Hansard tomorrow. I believe the fishermen have been cheated this year on a wholesale scale and some recompense or rebate ought to be given to the fishermen if the merchants have made the exorbitant profit which the fishermen think, and which I think, they have made on the sale of much of the fish. The fishermen had to sell their fish quickly and when they did so they did it at a great sacrifice. It is not right that the merchants should be able to profit by the great difference between the price which the fishermen received in many cases and which the bureau of statistics shows was received.
In 1929 the maritime provinces were in a great state of depression. The government appointed a commission under the late Judge MacLean, I believe, to go through the Gaspe peninsula and the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island to investigate the poverty and the generally bad conditions that prevailed amongst fishermen. As a result a report was brought in and one of the recommendations contained therein was that it was time for fishermen to be organized in co-operative societies. It was recommended that the federal government should appoint an organizer to go down there, carry on educational work and organize the fishermen into co-operative societies. I have a copy of that

report and I shall read a few sentences from it to show you what they recommended. They are:
We recommend, therefore, that the establishment of co-operative organizations of fishermen be assisted by the department as soon, as possible, and that an organizer, experienced in co-operative methods, be appointed and paid by the federal government for the required period to initiate and complete this work, A preliminary study and survey of the entire maritime provinces should be made to determine the localities where such organizations are possible or feasible. We do not conceive such an undertaking to be beyond the scope of departmental responsibility or government aid. The fisheries are a basic industry and are reasonably entitled to assistance and encouragement. A similar venture has already been aided for agriculture, in part at least. We are far from suggesting that the government should enter into the business of buying and selling fish products; we merely suggest, rather, that it should help fishermen through their organizations to buy and sell for themselves to better advantage.
Then they go on to say that if they may judge from the success of similar undertakings in Canada, they feel that in a very short time these suggested co-operative undertakings will give good results. That was done; that recommendation was implemented, and the greatest expert on co-operatives on this continent, Right Rev. Dr. Moses Coady of Antigonish, was sent around the maritime provinces to organize the fishermen. As a result of his work the united maritime fishermen's association was established, and is functioning today.
What is to prevent the government doing the same thing in 1951 for Newfoundland? All that is necessary is for the minister to appoint a man to go to Newfoundland and organize the fishermen; and it should be done quickly, before the 1951 season begins. I am sure all the members here from Newfoundland and the maritime provinces will realize that unless the fishermen are organized they are defenceless against the merchants, especially when they come to sell their catch. I trust, therefore, that the minister will give serious consideration to what I have suggested, remembering that, as I have said previously in this house, what counts in the fishing industry is the fisherman. He is the one who must be benefited. If he is not, the system is a failure. If the fisherman is going to be disgruntled and dissatisfied, as he is this year, selling off his equipment, selling his vessels, stuck on the rocks, as they say at home, for the fishing season, then we would have been better off under our own government, because we never would have allowed the fishermen to suffer as they have been suffering for the past year. I saw men with reputations as great fish killers at home on the rocks in Newfoundland, their beautiful vessels lying in the harbour, because they could not get supplies to go fishing. Even then they were not as badly off as those who 80709-to i
The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne did go fishing. Many of those who brought in catches had to sell them at depressed prices, as I have attempted to show.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope the minister will consider what the fisherman has to say, and not listen only to the fisheries board, or the salt cod export board, or the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited. As I say, the first thing to do is send someone down there to organize them, and they could very easily be amalgamated with the fishermen of Nova Scotia. The advantages of co-operation are well known in Newfoundland today, because many of the bankers from the maritime provinces come into the harbour of St. John's and other harbours along the coast and tell the fishermen in Newfoundland what they are being paid for fish in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. In almost every case we have found that the price being paid in Nova Scotia is better than the price the Newfoundland fisherman is receiving, and I say that is largely the result of the organization of the fishermen.
Now, sir, for the remainder of my time I propose to deal with the international situation. I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Breton) on his excellent speech in seconding the motion for an address in reply. I am sorry that I do not know French well enough to have the courage to address these remarks to him in his own language, but I may tell him I have read his speech with interest and noted his emphasis on the provincial and federal arrangements mentioned in the speech from the throne. I also noted with interest his historical reference to the fact that this year represents the fifteenth centenary of the invasion of the civilized world by the unholy alliance of the Slavs and Mongols. Everyone here acquainted with ancient history knows what destruction the ancient Roman empire suffered when those terrible races overran Italy and Gaul, as the hon. member said; and he pointed out that today the danger is much greater.
Then I should like to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on his very interesting speech. Whatever we may think of his decisions I believe we agree that the hon. gentleman makes a very interesting speech, not merely one that you delight to listen to at the time it is given but one you can pick up later and enjoy not only the phraseology but the fine distinctions he draws. I was particularly struck with the fine distinctions he made in his speech the other day. I do not believe the ordinary citizen of this country is able to follow those fine distinctions, however; nor do I believe the ordinary citizen of this

The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne country is able to follow the complicated debates that have been taking place in the United Nations assembly for the past few months. The ordinary citizen is not able to appreciate the niceties of the thing at all. Therefore he becomes disinterested and a little impatient with what is going on. He can see the broad issues, but I suppose the finer ones must be left to the experts. The ordinary citizen therefore is dependent to a large extent upon those propounders of public opinion, the ministers of the government and the editors of the newspapers.
In listening to the Secretary of State for External Affairs it seemed to me there was a lack of realism about his speech. He said, as is true, that the free world is in the greatest possible danger; and I commend this to my hon. friend who preceded me. If words mean anything, that meant we ought to be almost frightened to death. The free world is in the greatest possible danger; nothing could be greater than the greatest possible danger. How long has that situation existed? How long did it take the members of the United Nations to determine how the conduct of the Chinese should be designated? Let us compare the time it took to determine what name should be applied to the conduct of North Korea. We remember the special session, at which we were presented with a white paper entitled "Canada and the Korean Crisis". Let me direct the attention of the house to page 7 of that publication:
. . . the United States government informed the secretary general of the United Nations on June 25 that it considered the attack of the North Korean forces on the republic of Korea constituted "a breach of the peace and an act of aggression" and urgently requested the calling of an immediate meeting of the security council, the whole machinery and the first purpose of the United Nations was put to the test.
A meeting was called for that very day; before the day was over North Korea was declared to be an aggressor, and an immediate request went out to the member governments of the United Nations for assistance. Because the United States was the only country on hand with forces to repel this North Korean attack, the government of the United States sent those forces immediately.
On the other hand, how long did it take to decide that China was an aggressor? We were told that this action by the United Nations was something new, something historic, something we should all remember; that a new era was dawning for the world. More than once we were told, by ministers in this house and by people in other countries, that this was police action. Well, having been a magistrate for a number of years I am familiar with what is meant by police action. Let me contrast the ordinary procedure in a

police action with what has taken place in regard to Korea and China. If a citizen is assaulted on the street, what does he do? He cries for help; if there is a policeman within' a block or two someone will say, "You had better get down there; a man is being attacked," and the policeman gets there as quickly as he can. Or someone telephones the police station and the black maria, as we call it at home, or the police wagon is sent out and if possible the attacker is arrested. In other words the police go into action as quickly as possible. What happened in Korea? The call went out that the South Korean territory was invaded and that the North Koreans had attacked an unprepared and unsuspecting country. The United Nations was the magistrate that was appealed to and that asked for the police to come. The first police to arrive on the scene were the United States forces. Other policemen came up after a while. Through the skilful manoeuvres of the chief of that police force, General MacArthur, the assault was quelled and it looked as if the whole thing was over. However, it was not over. We were wrong.
Suppose that, when the police went to assist an ordinary citizen', the bystanders took a part in the affair; what would happen then? They would be arrested also, and the bystanders who assaulted the police would be liable to a second charge, they would be liable not merely to one charge but to two charges. Whereas the original aggressors or assailants would be charged with assault and battery, the second assailants would be charged with interfering with the police in the performance of their duty and would be liable to another two years' imprisonment in addition to the three years for which they would be liable for assault.
What happened as to the police action in Korea when the bystanders, who were well prepared to attack, came in? With the intervention of the Chinese communist army, did the United Nations immediately take action against them and lay a further charge? No, they did not. But in my humble opinion, and I believe in the opinion of a great many people, there was a great deal of shillyshallying and beating about the bush; it was said that we did not know this and that we did not know that. In my opinion the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has added a new conundrum to the puzzle book. What he has done is this. He has found an answer to the question: When is an aggressor not an aggressor? The answer, as I conceive it to be from his remarks, is: When the aggression is an old one. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the old aggression was finished and done with and that there was a new aggression. I will admit that the

Secretary of State for External Affairs was perhaps placed in a difficult position; but for the life of me I do not see how he can call it an old aggression when an army that has been poised on the Manchurian border attacked the police force of the United Nations, the hope of the civilized world, and caused them so many hundreds and even thousands of casualties.
In this subamendment we are asked to condemn the action of the United Nations in declaring that communist China was an aggressor. It seems to me that if we accept that subamendment, what it amounts to is that the members of this house are declaring that the United Nations are aggressors, because where two people are into a fight, one of them must be an aggressor. I repeat that statement: If we accept that subamendment of the C.C.F. party, it amounts to an acknowledgment that the United Nations themselves were the aggressors in this matter.
I have here another document, a white paper distributed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. On pages 9 and 10 of it are listed the different dates and the events that took place on those dates which justified the United Nations in deciding that communist China was an aggressor. I notice here an extraordinary thing-I do not know whether other hon. members have noticed it -and I do not know what significance it has. I notice on October 30:
Interrogation of 19 Chinese prisoners of war identified two additional regiments of 124 CCF division . . .

I am not making any suggestions at all. There are the facts and there is the document presented by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. At page 55 of Hansard the Secretary of State for External Affairs is reported to have said:
I feel, however, that the Far Eastern problems could be more readily solved if diplomatic relations existed with the government of China, which has the whole of the mainland of China under its control.
He made that statement of his feelings, but he did not back it up with any facts. I should like to know from the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he can give us any illustration in history which
The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne justifies him in saying that diplomatic relations with Russia or with any of the satellite countries have solved any problems whatsoever. Let me mention a few. Has the existence of diplomatic relations with Russia solved the question of Russia's foreign debt? Has it been able to give Christians living in Russia due respect for their religious beliefs and protection of their religion? Has it facilitated investigation of complaints against the Russian government or the question of the marriage of Russians with non-Russians? Has it solved the question of the disappearance of the 10,000 Polish officers who disappeared after they had been taken prisoners by Russia in 1939? Has it solved the question of the repatriation of the hundreds of thousands of German and Japanese prisoners of war, of whom no trace has been found since they were taken prisoners in the second world war? Has the existence of diplomatic relations with the friendly communist Yugoslavs enabled justice to be done as we should like to see it done, in accordance with the fundamental freedoms that we hear so much about, in the case of the arrest, the persecution, the trial and the imprisonment of Archbishop Stepinac? Has the existence of diplomatic relations with these communist dictatorships and totalitarian regimes helped in any way to prevent espionage, sabotage and underground revolutionary activities in all the other countries?
We all recognize that there are fundamental differences of outlook and differences in belief between the governments of communist countries and our own. The chief difference is that communism is materialistic and atheistic. It recognizes neither the divine origin of the universe nor the divine destiny of man. It is built on hate rather than on love. And they were referring to the socialist
members in Great Britain. I continue:
-or self-delusion of persons or groups who hesitate to choose between the proletariat and the bourgeoisie; who hesitate between a life-and-death struggle and the role of assistants to the expiring bourgeoisie.
Now, sir, the effect of voting for this subamendment would be, as I have said, to brand the United Nations organization as aggressors.
The aim of communism is world domination. That has been so often stated by the Russians themselves that we are fools to think otherwise. The general opinion that prevails today is that the greatest danger lies in the west, and I believe that opinion to be sound. Because of long civil wars in China and the war of attrition with Japan, China cannot be in a position to make war on any great scale.
If there is a surrender to aggression and the use of force, it will be not only a military defeat but a moral defeat, the results of which may be catastrophic.
Today in Japan there are 84 million people watching anxiously what is taking place. It seems to me, unless Korea is re-established at least in the position it was before June 25, with compensation, if possible, from the North Koreans, the United Nations is not able to fulfil its task.
In conclusion, sir, I should like to draw your attention to a press dispatch that appeared in a St. John's, Newfoundland, paper on January 21. I am not sure that it appeared in other papers. It came from Berlin and it said:
An 18-year-old German's defiant cry that he would rather die than bow to communist rule stirred his countrymen today on both sides of the iron curtain.
"I love my freedom more than my life," Herman Joseph Flade shouted to a communist court in Russian-controlled Dresden.
That was courage, Mr. Speaker. Does not that outburst of that condemned but courageous German represent the feelings of us all?
