Some hon. gentleman earlier in this debate made the statement that in his opinion this session of the House of Commons would be devoted largely to the discussion of international affairs. To some extent I agree with him; but I think his attention should be called to the fact that there are many weighty


matters of domestic concern which will have to be debated and discussed during the present session.
To some extent I am inclined to agree with him because it is impossible to get a true picture of the over-all situation of Canada at the present time unless one gives at least some consideration to the relationship of Canada to the United Nations organization and to world affairs.
Just over 30 years ago in this house I opposed the subscription of Canada to the covenant of the league of nations; and some years later, in 1923, I introduced a resolution calling upon Canada to withdraw from the league of nations. Nevertheless I cannot claim the prescience of having opposed the entry of Canada into the United Nations organization because at that time the wave of idealism for the brotherhood of man and of enthusiasm swept the world and encompassed Canada itself. But permit me to say, sir, as one who has never made any claim to an extensive or intensive study of external affairs, and who knows no more of the proceedings of the United Nations than that which he gleaned from the headlines in newspapers or from the radio commentators, that in my humble opinion, whatever may be said in favour of the United Nations organization -and much can be said and has been said by its supporters and apologists-certainly we can no longer say that it will bring about peace in this world. Nor can it be said that the United Nations of itself can prevent aggression by a major power or its satellites.
In order to endeavour to assure ourselves of a somewhat uneasy peace we are obliged perhaps not to disregard the United Nations organization but at least to set it aside in favour of the Atlantic treaty. Let me say at the outset of my remarks on this subject that I favour the Atlantic treaty; but let me also say that in placing most of our faith and confidence on what can be accomplished out of that pact and that treaty we are returning to that which we have condemned and reviled in the past, namely, power politics.
I can see little or no difference between the state of the world as it exists at the present time and the state of the world as it was immediately prior to and during the seven years war, the Napoleonic wars and the first world war. Now as then, nations, desiring to preserve their autonomy and their liberty against the encroachment of mon-archial or dictatorial tyrants, had been obliged to band themselves together in combinations or coalitions; now, as in that time, the weaker nations are obliged to call on the

stronger ones for subsidies for arms, and for the furnishing of armed forces.
Now, as in former times, there are satellite wars and undeclared wars. Prior to the seven years war the English were fighting the French in America, and the French were fighting the English in India for months and perhaps years, long before their governments and courts declared that a state of war existed. So that if my conjecture is the right one, and we are dependent almost entirely, for the preservation of peace in the world and for the prevention of aggression, upon the construction of a wall of peace against Russian aggression in Europe, then we have returned to the realm of world politics and of power politics.
As I said before, I am not opposing the Atlantic pact; but I would like it to be placed in its true light before the people of this country, and before the members of the house. I believe that at the present time the combination of the Atlantic nations is probably the only thing which will save the liberties of the European nations, at any rate, and probably save their hides.
I realize, as every member realizes, that the Atlantic nations, particularly those in Europe, in banding themselves together to resist aggression are taking upon themselves a very grave risk. But it is what Mr. Churchill called in the last war a calculated risk. It is a calculation that fear of the atomic bomb may deter Russia for a sufficient length of time to enable the Atlantic nations to rearm. And, less probably, it is a risk calculated on the fact that perhaps Russia, with the diverse elements of nations and races which compose it, has not as yet formed herself into a nation so well integrated as to permit of undertaking a global war. The Atlantic nations, those who subscribe to the pact, and who live on this side of the Atlantic, have come to the conclusion, rightly or wrongly, that they cannot afford to allow Russia to sweep over Europe, and to become possessed of the manpower and industrial potential which is on that continent. As a result of that, these nations have decided to extend their frontiers to the other side of the Atlantic, by extending assistance in the way of armament and equipment, and by rearming the peoples of Europe.
The policy and program laid down last evening by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) is that, as a nation, we shall give our utmost support to the Atlantic pact nations, that we shall do so by supplying arms and equipment, by placing our industrial potential at their disposal, and by sending armed forces to Europe.
With respect to the program which was so well explained by the minister himself last
The Address-Mr. Power night, it seems to me that the first reaction of the house and of the Canadian people must have been one of astonishment at the magnitude and cost of the program he unfolded. It drove home to us, and I think to the people of Canada, that in order even to prepare for war we must spend almost astronomical sums. If that be the case, if the preparation in order to deter the enemy from attacking us runs us into five billions of dollars, then it is difficult to imagine what a real war would cost.
The next reaction-and this is the one which struck me-is that it behooves us to have a certain note of caution. We should- and I gather the government has given consideration to these things-endeavour to ascertain for ourselves, as Canadians, how we may be of the most assistance to our partners in the Atlantic pact, if we are to play fully the role we propose to play. And the note of caution I would wish to sound would be this: Having decided on the course of action and on the program which we should follow in order best to render assistance, let us be careful not to waste our energies and our resources by an overdiversification of those energies and resources.
I take it for granted, indeed I think the minister so stated, that the decisions arrived at as to the kind of assistance we propose to render to our partners were decisions which had been approved of and agreed upon-subject of course to confirmation by parliament-by our partners in the Atlantic pact. Canada, by agreement with the Atlantic pact nations, apparently has decided to give preponderance in its assistance to air power. It will do this, firstly, by training the air crews of its associates, and secondly by furnishing squadrons to Europe. Apparently our allies are satisfied with this proposed contribution. The question I ask myself is whether the people of Canada will be satisfied with this contribution of a preponderance in air forces. I say that because, during world war II, there were persons in the country and even in the House of Commons who, notwithstanding the glamour and the glory of the achievements of the air force, and notwithstanding that, in proportion to the number of their men actively engaged, they suffered greater casualties than any other arm of the service, were not convinced that Canada was doing its part in that war, until such time as casualty reports came rolling in from Italy.
I am not saying I blame those people. There are in Canada a number of men who are battery-minded, battalion-minded, division-minded; and they have as much right to their opinions as anyone else. Then there

The Address-Mr. Power are other hon. members of the house and other men in this country who believe in a big navy.
I expect to be accused of being prejudiced, but I put myself on the side of the angels, geographically speaking-I favour the Royal Canadian Air Force. Since we are now laying down government policy for the next three years, a policy which presumably will be followed should we be so unfortunate as to be drawn into a shooting war, it should be part of the duty of every hon. member of this parliament, before allowing this program to pass unchallenged, to explain his views and state whether he considers it to be in the interests of Canada to have a greater proportion of the strength of Canada devoted to an air force than to any other force.
I say that advisedly because I well remember at the beginning of world war II when the delegates from Great Britain came here to propose that we embark upon a great air training scheme. The then minister of finance, my late chief, a leader and patriot whose like has rarely been seen in this house, Layton Ralston, said to the delegates that we should be careful to be sure that Canada could afford this large amount of money and, secondly, that Canada should not be bled white right at the start of the war. He pointed out further to the delegates that we were likely to have other commitments, that we were likely to have to furnish ground forces. The reply was made that the primary duty of Canada was to undertake this great air training scheme.
As time went on we all know how that air training scheme was developed, but other efforts were put forth paralleling that scheme. Not only did they cost enormous sums of money, but in the long run it led to serious difficulties.
I mention these things in order that we in this house, as well as the people in the country, may thoroughly understand this program. As I said before, I strongly favour a preponderance of assistance by way of an air force. Since I am asking other hon. members to give their reasons why they would favour a big navy, a big army, a big tank brigade or preference for other components of an army, perhaps I should give some of the reasons I have for suggesting that an air program should be adopted. I say this notwithstanding what may appear to have been a setback at the beginning of the Korean war. Perhaps the supporters of a great air force held exaggerated views and possibly the effectiveness of air strength did not come up to their expectations, but I do believe,


and I think this is admitted, that supremacy in the air will go a long way toward settling any future war.
The reasons I have for supporting an air program are that Canadians for some reason or other have a great reputation as air warriors; that Canada has earned a reputation for its capacity to train air crew; that the program calls for Canadian squadrons, manned by Canadians and supplied with Canadian equipment from Canadian factories.
Perhaps I am treading on dangerous ground when I contend that there is less danger of deterioration of morale among air force personnel stationed in a foreign country than there is on the part of, let us say, army personnel. I think it will be confirmed by those who were fortunate to be in England during the first two and a half or three years of the war that it was extremely difficult to keep up the morale of the ground troops no matter how well the manoeuvres simulated actual conditions of warfare. There is always the danger of boredom with a consequent loss of morale.
But as far as the air force are concerned, the ground crew will be doing exactly the same work they would be doing in wartime. They will be preparing aircraft for troops. Perhaps the danger will not be so great as if an enemy were shooting at them, but they must be ever alert to any deficiency in the machinery or equipment. The air crew are engaged in a hazardous occupation. Every young man who makes up part of an air crew has the pleasure of having under his hand a fast, swiftly moving machine. For these reasons I believe there is less danger of deterioration in their morale.
Undoubtedly there would be an easier interchange of squadrons. Those which are trained here in Canada could more readily, more efficiently and more expeditiously be exchanged with squadrons being trained on the other side. With respect to the psychological effect on our allies and1 on our enemies, which is given as one of the great reasons why we should send forces to Europe, the greater mobility of the air arm and the fact that there will be a large number of men engaged in servicing and in flying eleven squadrons would result in their making their presence felt equally with and perhaps more than an equivalent or similar number of the other arms of the services. Perhaps I should not say this as a last reason, but if the worst comes to the worst the air force has half a chance of getting out and coming back again.
I assume that the division-which is a new term to me in air force jargon-mentioned by the minister will be composed of fighters, interceptors, reconnaissance and transport. It

is a matter of regret to me that it will be almost impossible to add squadrons or wings or groups of bombers. Although I have not gone to any authoritative source, I am informed that to have in Great Britain or on the continent of Europe a group similar in size and equipment to No. 6 Canadian bomber group in the last war would cost in initial equipment alone anything from $1,500 million to $2 billion. Therefore we are precluded by the very thought and consideration of the cost of any such contribution of heavy bombers.
I am told that an individual heavy bomber costs anywhere from $5 million to $6 million. Therefore a squadron composed of twenty bombers would cost in equipment alone $100 million. Therefore the task of strategic bombing of the enemy will, as I understand it, be left largely to the air force of the United States of America just as the task of supplying ground forces will apparently be placed to a considerable extent on the shoulders of the republic of France.
There is one other matter that I should like to mention, and since it is one that has aroused some controversy in this house and outside I approach it with considerable diffidence. It is the question of whether or not a committee of this house should be set up to discuss the expenditure on national defence. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has set forth his views on the matter eloquently and cogently. Members of the government have replied equally eloquently and in terms which merit consideration. I am inclined to think that there is a middle course between the views of the government and those of some of the members of the opposition.
With respect to the constitutional aspect, I believe that matters relating to policies and strategy are the responsibility of the government and the government alone. Recently I was reading the life of William Pitt, Earl of Chatham, by Brian Tunstall, and I found this passage in reference to the government of William Pitt:
In a country such as England, governed by a constitutional monarchy, it is neither desirable nor practical for war to be conducted either jointly or independently by the heads of the fighting services. On all major issues they must receive express direction from the crown constitutional advisers, responsible to parliament. Admirals and generals are the commanders-in-chief of the sea and land forces, but the crown and ministerial advisers are the commanders-in-chief of the whole nation.
I believe it will be found that Lloyd George in world war I and Winston Churchill in world war II kept within their own hands all decisions with respect to policy and strategy, and I can conceive of nothing worse for the morale and discipline of the various armed
The Address-Mr. Power forces than for their chiefs of staffs to be called before a parliamentary committee to give evidence either for or against the policies laid down by the government. I will give one instance. I myself, although I was a member of the government when the project was initiated, have always had serious doubts as to the value to this country of the creation of a fleet air arm and of the acquisition of the Magnificent.
I hold those views and I believe that in all probability a great many of the superior officers of the Royal Canadian Air Force hold similar views, although I have not communicated with them for over five years, but I would not think it either fair to the forces or fair to the minister to call the chiefs of staff of the Royal Canadian Air Force before a parliamentary committee and to place them in contradiction with the policy of the government. I would go one step further. In my time there were in the Royal Canadian Air Force earnest, conscientious and devoted men who had strong views as to certain types of equipment. Those views were fought over and discussed in air council and sometimes went as far as defence council, but once the policy was settled, once the chiefs of staff and the officers concerned had decided that such a type of equipment should be that which would be acquired and no other kind, then the matter rested there.
I think it would be unfair to place officers of different arms of the services in contradiction with each other with respect to such matters. That is only a personal view acquired from some little experience in dealing with this department.
On the other hand it seems to me that since we are embarking upon a program calling for the expenditure of $5 billion, this House of Commons of Canada has a duty to scrutinize and supervise that expenditure. It is extremely difficult for that scrutiny and supervision to be carried out in a house composed of as many members as we have here; and I believe that if a committee on expenditure were set up, with an appropriate reference which could be agreed upon by the leaders of the government and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), much good would result. Members of parliament would be in a better position to analyse and understand why certain moneys were being expended.
I would not propose to curtail in any way the right of every member of parliament to talk on any subject arising out of this expenditure; nor would I implement the rule, if it ever was a rule, that was brought into effect some years ago to prevent questions being placed on the order paper with respect to a department whose affairs were under the

The Address-Mr. Gosselin scrutiny of a committee of this house. Either by arrangement among the members of this house or by the order of reference I would safeguard in every possible way the rights of members of parliament to discuss anything arising out of the estimates of the Department of National Defence. At the same time I believe that a more careful scrutiny of these expenditures, having in mind the complexities which are bound to arise in connection with an expenditure of this size, could be made by setting up such a committee. This I believe would maintain the traditions of parliament and at the same time would be a benefit to the members and to the people of this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I join other hon. members of the house in extending my congratulations to the mover (Mr. McMillan) and seconder (Mr. Breton) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, who performed their duties so well. I am sure the counties they represent will be highly pleased by the way they carried out their task.
In my first remarks I do not intend to deal at length with the matter of national defence, but I believe it is my duty to express my views with respect to the most important matters with which this government will be called upon to deal during the present session. I have listened carefully to the various speeches that have been made since the opening of the session and the statements by the different ministers, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and others. From the very first Canada has been developed on certain principles and traditions, and we wish to continue under those principles. Canada has a small population, but we have always known freedom and good understanding, and we intend to maintain our freedom against any aggressors who would destroy it.
I believe it is our duty to treat this matter in a non-political way. I believe it is the responsibility of every member of this house to deal with these matters sincerely and honestly. On various occasions our representatives at the United Nations have stated that these principles should be advanced throughout the world, and we have felt it our duty to join with other countries to find ways and means of making sure that communist principles shall not be introduced here. From what I have read in the newspapers and learned in other ways I want to congratulate those members of the government who have had the responsibility of expressing the principles in which our country believes. It is our duty to give them our entire support day 

by day, so they may be in a position to act immediately if at any time they feel the welfare of the country is threatened.
As I say, we have only a small population compared with other members of the United Nations, but in the last two wars we have shown the world that when the Canadian people undertake a task they fulfil it one hundred per cent. We intend to carry on in the same tradition if there should be a third world war, but I believe we should be prepared to assist the United Nations in every possible way so that the danger of a third world war may be averted.
It is our duty, Mr. Speaker, as these matters are presented to the house to scrutinize and examine them, but in the most sincere way, so that no errors may be committed; and with our experience in the last war I believe we should strike an average of almost one hundred per cent in our endeavours with the United Nations. We have an energetic population which is ready to make all possible sacrifices in order that our liberties and our way of life may be preserved. The efforts of our people, with all our natural resources, will be offered to the United Nations, if necessary, so that success may be achieved. We must endeavour to make every possible sacrifice in our way of living so that we shall be able to meet the expenditures necessary to carry on the fight to preserve our principles. I shall not endeavour to go into the ways and means of administering the various departments, for I have not the necessary knowledge or experience. Nevertheless, I feel that those who have the knowledge of these matters should be supported one hundred per cent, in order that success may be achieved.
Our sister country on this side of the ocean, with a large population, has up to the present time taken measures to protect freedom and liberty, so that the principles of the communists who desire to rule the world will not be accepted amongst the free nations. Knowing our obligations, we in Canada for several months past have followed the contribution which Canada has proposed to make to ensure the success of the United Nations. In this I believe we have the support of the entire population of Canada. They feel that it is the duty of the government, through their representatives, to follow every move which is necessary and to give the necessary financial support regardless of politics; because liberty cannot be bought with dollars but can be obtained only by defending the principles which we are endeavouring to preserve.

Along with the measures we take for our defence, it is our duty to carry on under our social laws which have been on the statute books for several years past, so our people will be assured that, during their lives, they will be protected by social laws designed to help those who have not been so fortunate as to accumulate wealth and who are most in need. By so doing we shall establish in this country of ours the basis of the principles which we have for many years been supporting.
It is our duty, Mr. Speaker, to base our policies on the development of our natural resources. This development will be necessary in our efforts in connection with national defence. It is necessary for us to create in the minds of our younger generation the feeling that the policy which this government is bound to follow is one looking to their protection in the future. It is our duty to see that our natural resources are developed as fast as possible so that our growing population will feel convinced that there is for them a living in this country.
It is also our duty to encourage in every way possible the principles of labour. With regard to those principles of labour, may I say a few words of thanks to this government for the action taken by them with regard to the railroad strike. I am a railway employee and I confess that I was a striker. We have obtained entire satisfaction, and I am speaking in the name of a large number of railroad employees who have said that they were entirely satisfied with the way in which this government acted. The railroad men had the right, and they exercised it, to tie up the transportation system of Canada; and I wish to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for ordering the railroad men to go back to work. We had the right to tie up the transportation of the Canadian people, and the government has given us the right to negotiate further, and we have obtained satisfactory results. I wish to thank the entire membership of this house for granting us the privilege of continuing those negotiations.
Furthermore, I think it is my duty as a farmer to offer to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) my congratulations on the way he is carrying on in the interests of the Canadian people. Whether you are from the east or from the west, the interests of agriculture are intimately connected. We are working for the interests of the Canadian people. It is the duty of the Minister of Agriculture and of this government to establish markets so that our products can be
The Address-Mr. Gosselin sold as they are grown. Agricultural products cannot be preserved from year to year. They must be sold after the crop has been harvested. It is necessary for the farmers to obtain immediate payment. It is necessary for the farmers to be protected, as they are the fundamental basis of the prosperity of the country. It is necessary that the farmers obtain all the encouragement possible so that they may enjoy the comforts they deserve for the hours of work they perform.
I would not say that the farmers are not prosperous at the present time, but I will say that we need further protection having regard to the preservation of our products. I have all confidence that the Minister of Agriculture will give his full support to obtaining refrigerating processes so that our pork, our eggs, our poultry products and so on may be displayed and sold at the proper time, and at a reasonable price, to the * benefit cf the labouring population.	.
I believe it is the duty of the Department of Agriculture to study ways and means of increasing production. If we can do this, we shall be able to reduce the cost of living. It is necessary that production be increased, and this can only be done by giving credit to the farmers, as has already been done in many different ways by the Department of Agriculture. I feel that additional ways should be found of giving further protection to our farmers. May I repeat that it was a great pleasure to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture, who is a farmer himself, upon handling our agricultural matters in such a way that we can produce with confidence and that prices will be well protected. The farming industry faces great problems. If our farmers are not given the necessary encouragement to induce the younger element to remain on the soil, they will not do so. Our younger population are deserting the soil because they are not receiving sufficient remuneration for the work they perform. That difficulty could be overcome by giving our farmers a guaranteed price for their products. A guaranteed price would bring about such results as would encourage them to continue farming. Regardless of what the amount of subsidies may be, we must encourage the younger element to remain on the farms; otherwise it will be a disaster for our Canadian population.
Agriculture is still the basic industry of the country. We must be prepared for an increase in population, but we must also be in a position to produce the necessary supplies for the population whom we shall be called upon to support. If our farmers

The Address-Mr. Larson receive fair prices for their products, ways and means will be found to take care of the amounts required for national defence.
Before closing my remarks I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) whether it will not be possible to grant subsidies to the eastern parts of the country to enable the farmers to buy fertilizer. Our farms in the east require fertilizer. They require substances to destroy the acid which is gradually appearing in our soil. If the farmers could buy fertilizer at a cheaper rate, it would assist in increasing che productivity of the soil, and enable them co sell their produce at lower prices, because with the greater production the return for the work performed would be proportionately greater. At the same time our labour population would be able to buy produce at a lower price, and one more in keeping with the salaries they receive.
May I address a few words to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who is carrying on a great work in the improvement of the health of our people. Canada, like other countries, has to suffer from diseases amongst our population. It is necessary to call attention to this problem and to that of education. An unhealthy and an uneducated population is a detriment to any country. The policies which the department and the government are carrying out will help to maintain good understanding amongst the people of our country, and I am sure we are all glad to support them.	'
I believe every Canadian is willing to support the principle of taxation when necessary, and is willing to do all that is necessary so that we may maintain the principles under which the United Nations was formed and bring about good understanding and harmony amongst the nations of the world.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In this
debate, which hinges chiefly upon defence and on the diplomatic side of our national activities, I rise not because one so new as myself can attempt to advise the people who have had long experience in these things, but the speech from the throne and the remarks of the mover of the address in reply touched on a topic which was very interesting to me and, I feel, very vital to the future conduct of world policy.
I understand that when the first atomic explosion was carried out in Nevada a large staff of men was there to try to stop any reaction which might have occurred from the explosion of the bomb. That did not happen. The atomic bomb was developed. Scientists very soon decided that possibly they could use that atomic bomb to start reaction in some less volatile substance.

Possibly the hydrogen bomb is a fact. I do not know. It has never been officially declared a fact.
Is it impossible that some day scientists may figure out a method of using the same sort of knowledge to start some inert substance such as the air we breathe, or the soil we walk on, and end the whole course of human development on this planet? Trusting, however, that things will not be quite as serious as that, we can look forward in this country to the possibility of atomic attack.
There are some people in this country who say that we are totally unprepared to meet any attack in force. Today quite a few members of parliament went down to Montreal, and there they saw something which I am sure convinced them that we are not totally unprepared, but on the contrary we are doing everything possible,. and we are doing it effectively, to protect ourselves and our friends in the Atlantic pact.
War today is a pretty terrible thing. Centuries ago Athens and Sparta, the one a democratic country and the other a military-minded country, fought it out. I suppose people a few hundred miles away from what was going on, and who were not involved, did not even realize that there was a war on; but in this day and age a major conflict between two major nations is a thing which should be absolutely unthinkable. I for one still believe and hope that the eventuality of a war, chiefly with atomic weapons, is a thing which we shall never see. What the solution is I do not know. There are a lot of people who talk about a world federation. We have some sort of world federation in the United Nations, but it has no sovereign authority. It has not a police force which is completely under the control of that body. The next thing to that we have is the Atlantic pact. That organization is in a somewhat different position, because we have recently appointed a supreme commander who will have armies and forces of various kinds under his control. Then if any nation-and probably this is unthinkable-within the Atlantic pact were to start any form of aggression, police action would be taken immediately.
If that type of thing could be developed to encompass most of the nations of the world we would have some chance of having a federation of world nations. All this may look difficult, and appear to be impossible; but I presume that the problems that beset the founders of the United States federation, and the Canadian confederation must have appeared to them to be almost insurmountable.

These matters are more or less academic.
I feel that Russia, or the international comin-form is using a weapon against us which is as old as humanity itself. It is a weapon of which we do not realize the full import- and we have good reason for not doing so. They are using this weapon chiefly in Asia at the moment, and making very good use of it indeed. The reason we do not understand it is that as a nation on this continent we have never been hungry. The cost of living is high-certainly it is high. But practically every family on the continent can set a good table and buy the clothes they need. They can house themselves, and on top of that enjoy some of the amenities of life. To the average Asiatic, the cost of living is probably beyond his earning capacity.
In the conclusions reached at the Colombo conference it was found that the average amount of food upon which the average Asiatic exists for a day is about the same as the normal adult on this side of the water would eat at any one normal meal. The amount of clothing the average Asiatic gets is far from adequate. I do not propose to go into the merits or demerits of the Colombo plan at this time. That plan is set out in a journal on trade and commerce, and it is available to all. The only comment I would make is that the purpose is to give technical assistance so as to increase food production in Asia. Possibly that plan should be extended to provide actual foodstuffs when there are surpluses on this hemisphere. At the present time we have in Canada among other surpluses large stocks of low-grade wheat. It is difficult to make standard milling flour out of such wheat and I am sure that probably within the next year and a half it will be sold for the consumption of livestock. With the situation in India today, I am sure the people there would be happy to have some of that wheat, even though it is not of a top milling grade. It would still provide nourishment.
In Canada we have been bothered by food surpluses from time to time. We have always felt that large surpluses on hand depressed the market and tended to bring about a recession in agriculture. The Americans have had that same difficulty, but it would seem to me that they are somewhat more advanced in their thinking. I believe they are going into "*he next crop year with several hundred million bushels of wheat in surplus. However, rather than consider it a surplus which would depress the market, they consider it as a strategic war material, and one absolutely vital if an emergency arises.
We could allow Asiatic countries to carry on as best they can, as we have done in the
The Address-Mr. Larson past. We could allow situations to develop in China, as indeed they have developed, and take no responsibility for them. We can even watch the Chinese in vast numbers joining the communist armies, perhaps as a result of having been bribed to enter those armies, with the threat of starvation if they did not come in and promise of adequate food supplies if they did. With our supremacy in technical knowledge and industrial capacity we could probably defeat those huge armies; but to organize the military strength to fight and, when the time comes, to wipe out the hordes of people in those armies would cost us vast sums of money and a great deal of hardship through having to see our people go to war.
If we want to get right down to considering this matter from a business standpoint, even if we wanted to ignore the fact that possibly we are our brothers' keeper, we could say that it would be cheaper to feed them than to fight them. That is my belief; and in that position I do not think we have any choice. I believe it is cheaper to feed them than to fight them, and I doubt if there will ever be peace until the threat of famine has been wiped from the face of the earth.
We might say we have done something in the past to provide foodstuffs for China when it was needed, and when we have had surpluses; but our tendency has been to deal through normal channels, with the big businessmen of China. I doubt very much if the average coolie has ever felt any beneficial effects from what we have done.
It is apparent that the communists have gone into China and stirred up the masses against the land owners and the wealthy people. They have given support to taking over the property of those people. There may have been enough food produced from those activities, so that the communists have not had to send very much from their own countries into China to keep the people satisfied thus far. Indeed, they have had the Chinese fighting their battles, with the only cost to Russia being that of perhaps a few aircraft and tanks. We are now in a position where, even though for a long time the Chinese have been considered our friends, we do not feel we can talk with them. However, we are still on good terms with India and with Pakistan. We are still on speaking terms with a good many other countries in southeast Asia.
In the near future it seems to me it would be to our advantage politically to give some practical indication that we are on the side of those people, that we are people of good will, and that we are prepared to help them in their troubles. It could be said that this

The Address-Mr. Larson continent simply has not the ability to feed Asia. I agree. But there is no doubt in my mind that we could vastly increase production on this continent. In fact, there are several projects we could construct which would have the effect of increasing production. There is development work we could do. There are lands in northern British Columbia, in the Peace River district where the rainfall is adequate and where the soil is suitable, but where at the present time there are no settlers. If that were not sufficient we could go ahead with the South Saskatchewan river project and 400,000 acres of submarginal land could be brought into production to produce a lot of food.
Industrial skill can do a tremendous lot to make our position more secure, but well-fed people normally do not want to join armies to fight. We should not rest in our endeavours as a highly developed civilization until we see the world completely inhabited with well-fed people. With the international situation being as it is I do not see how we can afford not to do everything possible with our industrial ability to see that our friends have what is necessary for them to fight in defence of our way of life.
But there is a danger that if we place too much strain on our internal economy and spread ourselves too thin we will not be effective in international affairs. That great Canadian, the late W. L. Mackenzie King, said once that rather than making tours of the war fronts his job was to stay in Canada to see to it that our internal economy was operating to the fullest extent in order to produce things for our friends. He felt that our great strength lay in no hitches developing in this country.
At the risk of boring you I am going to say how pleased I am that the British government has considered fulfilling the "have regard to" clause in the five year wheat pool contract. I know that when that clause has been fulfilled to the satisfaction of the western farmers, and I do not think their requests are unreasonable, those same western farmers will be much happier at having to pay heavy taxes in order to supply aeroplanes to Great Britain and to train air crew and do those other things which will cost much in excess of what they are asking from the British at the moment. They will be ready to do all that most willingly.
I am not going to mention any alternatives because I am confident the British government is sound and fair enough to see that justice is done. There are no other alternatives that could be mentioned at this time.
From November 20 of last year to January 13 of this year my information indicates that some $39,900,000 of defence contracts were


issued in Canada. I have not the Alberta figures but the contracts in Manitoba amounted to $1,200,000 with only $60,000 in Saskatchewan. Saskatchewan does not worry about defence contracts to any great degree because the people do not feel that that is their role. They feel that their place in the national economy is the providing of that strategic material, food. If that material is not supplied everything else breaks down.
I have heard it said that the Saskatchewan farmers are making so much money that they do not know what to do with it. I have heard it said in high places that prosperity is judged by income tax collections. It must be realized that Saskatchewan is primarily an agricultural province and its primary production is wheat which is sold to the wheat board. The wheat board is an agency of government and the income tax department is a department of government. It is reasonable to expect that information passes back and forth and the experts are able by means of mathematical calculations to tell what it costs to run a farm. With that factor in mind it is easy for those who collect income taxes to assess and collect all that is coming to the federal government in these taxes.
Another fact to be remembered is that those who pay large income taxes farm large tracts of land. They have been fortunate enough to obtain those tracts of land and are thus able to produce more economically than the small farmer. Consequently most of the income tax is paid by a small group of people in Saskatchewan. The great majority of the people in Saskatchewan fall into that other class which do not enjoy the same prosperity.
In closing I want to say that I support the policy of the government as laid down last night by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in his speech during this debate. I feel that with the lead given by those two men and their associates we will have the best possible guarantee we could get that we will have a smooth-working, well-integrated internal economy which will allow this country to produce the way we saw it producing today in Montreal. I have great faith that with a smoothly integrated economy and with large defence production we can do our part to carry out our obligations in connection with affairs that lie ahead. But I wish to stress that we must keep our own internal affairs solid so that it will be possible for us to give the most to our friends.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think at this time the Canadian people are concerned about two serious problems. The first is the very serious international situation and the second is the constantly rising cost of living. Before I proceed to deal with my main topic this evening I wish to say that I heartily endorse the remarks made by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) concerning the present international situation. I also endorse the excellent and incisive speech made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) in connection with the same question. In 1941 it had become apparent to the government of the day that something had to be done to curb the pressures on the economy due to the rapid expansion which had taken place at that time, and the gradual absorption of formerly unemployed resources into the stream of production. For various reasons the government decided that monetary and fiscal policies alone were insufficient to curb inflationary tendencies. Two alternatives faced the government at that time. The first was selective controls confined to a few basic commodities and the second was an over-all price ceiling on all goods and services with accompanying production and distribution controls.
The minister of finance of that day stated in the house on November 6, 1941, that the government had chosen the latter alternative. The introduction of the over-all price ceiling was announced by the prime minister of that day on October 18, 1941, and came into effect on December 1, 1941. As we all know, price ceilings were based on prices in the period from September 15 to October 11, 1941.
There is no question that at the conclusion of the war the Canadian people realized the advantages of price control legislation and the advantages of certain necessary subsidies to equalize and stabilize the cost of living. Canadians realized that price control was effective. They realized it was successful, and I think that generally speaking the Canadian people fully appreciated the value
The Address-Mr. Herridge of that policy. In addition to the people, the Liberal government of that day realized that the Canadian people were in favour of price controls and had realized their effectiveness, their successful operation, and their advantage to the large majority of working people of this country.
They realized that to such an extent that they based their election appeal of 1945 to some extent upon the value of the price control policy to the Canadian people prior to that date.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And nearly got beat.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the hon. member who interrupted me is not going to massage his ego by constant inane, innocuous and inconsequential interruptions. I should like to quote a few statements! made by leaders of the Liberal party and by the Liberal party itself just prior to the election of 1945, realizing as they did the opinion of the Canadian people with respect to the Liberal party price control policy during the war, which we all admit was excellent. The late prime minister, Right Hon'. Mackenzie King, in an article in Maclean's magazine of February 1, 1945, had this to say:
Immediately after the war the dangers of inflation may be even greater than they are now. The Canadian people cannot afford to sacrifice the benefits of wartime stabilization by relaxing controls too soon.
In the Halifax Herald and other dailies of June 5, 1945, nation-wide Liberal advertising contained the following:
Consumer goods soon to be available at 1941 prices.
Again in the Halifax Herald and other dailies of June 5, 1945, Liberal advertising contained the following:
Price ceiling-the purchasing power of your dollars maintained by the price ceiling under careful Liberal management.
Again nation-wide Liberal advertising in the dailies throughout this country on June 5, 1945, contained the following:
New low-cost housing . . . instalments as low as $9.58 per month under the new national housing plan.
My point in commenting on the advertisements of that date is to illustrate the fact that the government was fully aware of the opinion of the Canadian people with respect to their policy of price control and necessary subsidies that was in effect during the war. We find that, although election advertising and election literature of that time indicated the continuance of the price control policy, that policy was changed some seven months later. On January 31,	1946, the Prime

The Address-Mr. Herridge Minister announced the government's decontrol policy and on February 1, 1946, the first actual decontrol of prices took place on a long list of items, although few were necessities of life. This action continued until well on in the summer. Wage controls were eliminated by the end of the year. From that time on, the Canadian people have been subjected to constantly rising prices.
As we all know, the cost of living has gone up and up. By the end of 1948 complete decontrol had practically been accomplished. Under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, originally passed in 1945, the dominion government had been enabled to retain authority over prices, production, distribution and rental controls, but at each successive session of parliament this power was restricted until today the only powers remaining with the government under this act are those over rents.
Rising prices between the early part of 1946 and the latter part of 1948 created such a disturbance and such protests throughout the country that the government was forced to give some consideration to public opinion in that regard. In February, 1948, when, as the result of decontrol, prohibition of certain imports from the United States and other factors, prices were soaring, there was a great outcry for the reinstitution of price control legislation. The government's answer was to set up a House of Commons committee to study the question. We all remember the lengthy sittings of that committee and the report it made. Then a royal commission was established to find out why prices were going up. I remember sitting in this house and hearing the then member for Cariboo, Mr. William Irvine, saying when the commission was being established that it was like the government witnessing someone drowning. Instead of trying to prevent the tragedy they appointed a committee to find out where the water came from.
The royal commission reported on March 18, 1949, after investigating a number of industries. Although the investigation of the commission did not bring prices down by so much as a cent, they did come to some significant conclusions. Before proceeding with my brief remarks this evening I want to quote from their report to indicate some of the conclusions which, as I said before, are most significant for the Canadian people. In volume I, pages 27 and 28, dealing with monopolistic conditions, the commission reported as follows:
The tendency appears to be for monopolistic enterprises to try to protect themselves from the "peaks and valleys" of the business cycle by obtaining for themselves a stable price over a period of time, the net result of which is generally to place

the average price of their goods in the long run above what would be the average competitive level.
That is an example of the operation of the free enterprise system. Then the section dealing with mark-ups is very interesting for those interested in studying this important subject. Again I quote from volume 1, page 26:
In our investigations we found that it was general for the distributive trades to maintain the same fixed percentage mark-ups on their various lines of merchandise as their costs rose, and that the effect of this practice was to increase prices to the consumer much more than a dollar and cent mark-up would. Where a fixed percentage mark-up is used by the manufacturer, wholesaler and retailer, an initial cost increase at the manufacturing level is pyramided through the entire price structure . . .
I could give much lengthier quotations, but I am just giving a few to illustrate my point. Dealing with bread the report had this to say at page 29 of volume 1:
The margins now being established appear to be out of proportion with the margins that would exist under competitive conditions on a fast moving packaged food such as bread.
There again the obvious implication is that under this so-called free enterprise system we have a monopoly control avoiding the effects of even proper competition. Then, dealing with the situation concerning livestock, the report has this to say at page 31 of volume 1:
The very heavy capital investment required, together with decreasing cost ratio as the scale of the business expands, tends to keep additional competitors from entering the field . . .
Again there is the implication of monopolistic control in order to maintain prices; yet we are told repeatedly that members on the government side and members on the opposition side support a free enterprise economy. I have a few other references before I go on. The report of the commission dealing with monopolies in textiles has this to say, at page 33 of volume 1:
The returns on capital for the nylon producers and the second mentioned rayon manufacturer were, by any standard, very high indeed.
You must remember, Mr. Speaker, that this was the standard established by the royal commission. Again I quote from the report of the commission dealing with fertilizer monopolies, at page 33 of volume 1:
One firm, following decontrol, raised its domestic prices to export levels and more than tripled its percentage of net profits to capital employed between 1946 and early in 1948.

speechtext: How did they compete with you?

speechtext:
I thought I had finished with the hon. member, but apparently I have not. The point is that these advantages were taken of the Canadian people immediately following

the abolition of price control and the dropping of necessary subsidies. I could give many other references to show the advantage taken by many firms in this country of that policy of decontrol, but let us see what happened after the change of policy on the part of the government of the day. To illustrate, while the general wholesale price index went up 52 per cent between July, 1946, and July, 1950, the index of the wholesale prices of farm products went up only 35 per cent. Since the end of the war, farm products prices have risen less than prices of most other groups in the wholesale index.
